problem.title: Design a Distributed Rate Limiter
problem.prompt: Design a rate limiter for a public API that enforces per-user and per-IP request limits at scale. The service must handle high throughput, be deployable across multiple data center regions, and gracefully degrade when the rate-limiting backend is unavailable.
requirements: Enforce per-user and per-IP rate limits, such as 1,000 requests per minute per user.
Return HTTP 429 with retry guidance when a quota is exceeded.
Support per-second, per-minute, and per-hour windows.
Coordinate decisions across multiple API server instances.
Support configurable limits by API key tier and endpoint.
Define fail-open or fail-closed behavior when the rate-limit store is unavailable.
constraints: Peak API traffic is approximately 500,000 requests per second.
Rate-limit decisions should add no more than 2 ms at p99.
The limiter should provide shared enforcement across 10 or more API nodes in a region.
API processes do not share memory.
Regional enforcement is the default scope; strict global enforcement requires additional coordination.

stages.learnerPrompt: Identify the key requirements and constraints. What algorithms are candidates for rate limiting? What does 'distributed' add to the problem compared to a single-server limiter?

referenceMaterial.summary: Core tension: single-server counters don't work across nodes; distributed counters add network round-trips. The 2 ms latency budget is tight — a Redis call is typically 0.5–1 ms in the same data center. Algorithm choice (token bucket, fixed window, sliding window log, sliding window counter) affects accuracy, memory, and implementation complexity.
tradeOffs: Fixed window: simple, low memory, but allows 2× burst at window boundaries.
Sliding window log: accurate, but memory grows with request count per user.
Sliding window counter (hybrid): accurate within ~0.5% error, O(1) memory — best for most production systems.
Token bucket: handles bursts naturally; refill rate maps to sustained limit.

stages.learnerPrompt: Choose an algorithm and sketch a design for the distributed rate limiter. How do API nodes share state? How do you handle latency and failure?
Compare your design to the sliding window counter with Redis. Note similarities and differences.

referenceMaterial.summary: Sliding window counter backed by Redis. Each incoming request: compute window boundaries → INCRBY the current window counter for the key (userId:windowStart) → read previous window counter → compute weighted count = prevCount × (remaining fraction of prev window) + currCount → if weighted count > limit, return 429.
approachSteps: 1. Request arrives at API node with userId and timestamp.
2. Compute current 60-second window start: windowStart = floor(now / 60) * 60.
3. Redis MULTI: INCR user:{userId}:{windowStart}, GET user:{userId}:{windowStart-60}, EXPIRE user:{userId}:{windowStart} 120.
5. If weightedCount > limit: set X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0, return 429 with Retry-After header.
6. Else: decrement or allow — return 200 with X-RateLimit-Remaining header.
alternatives: Token bucket in Redis with Lua script: atomic, avoids race conditions, handles burst naturally. Slightly more complex Lua script to maintain.
Local in-memory limiter with gossip sync: low latency (no network call) but requires approximate counting — nodes can each allow up to limit/N individually, risking N× burst.
Centralized SQL counter: accurate but adds 5–20 ms per request — exceeds the 2 ms budget.
referenceMaterial.codeSnippet:
-- Atomic Redis Token Bucket Script (Runs in single-threaded event loop)
local tokens_key = KEYS[1]
local timestamp_key = KEYS[2]

local rate = tonumber(ARGV[1])      -- Refill rate (tokens per second)
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[2])  -- Maximum burst capacity
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])       -- Current epoch timestamp (seconds)
local requested = tonumber(ARGV[4]) -- Tokens requested (typically 1)

local current_tokens = tonumber(redis.call('get', tokens_key))
local last_refreshed = tonumber(redis.call('get', timestamp_key))

if current_tokens == nil then
  current_tokens = capacity
  last_refreshed = now
end

local delta = math.max(0, now - last_refreshed)
local tokens = math.min(capacity, current_tokens + (delta * rate))

if tokens >= requested then
  redis.call('set', tokens_key, tokens - requested)
  redis.call('set', timestamp_key, now)
  redis.call('expire', tokens_key, 3600)
  redis.call('expire', timestamp_key, 3600)
  return 1 -- Allowed
else
  return 0 -- Denied (HTTP 429)
end

stages.learnerPrompt: Why a sliding window over fixed window? Why Redis over a local in-memory counter? When would you choose fail-open vs fail-closed?

referenceMaterial.summary: Comprehensive evaluation of distributed rate limiting architecture: sliding window counters vs token buckets, centralized Redis clustering vs local in-process memory, atomic Lua script execution, and fail-open resilience.
tradeOffs: Sliding window vs fixed window: Fixed window allows up to 2× burst at the boundary (last second of window N + first second of window N+1). Sliding window eliminates this at O(1) memory cost.
Redis vs local counter: Local is O(0ms) but each node allows limit requests independently — 10 nodes allow 10× limit. Redis adds ~1 ms but provides a shared accurate counter.
Fail-open (allow on Redis failure): Protects availability; risk: abuse during outage. Use for non-critical APIs or when abuse impact is low.
Fail-closed (block on Redis failure): Protects against abuse; risk: legitimate users blocked during outage. Use for billing/sensitive APIs.
Lua scripts for atomicity: Redis MULTI/EXEC provides optimistic locking; Lua scripts provide true atomicity. For rate limiting, a Lua script is preferred to avoid race between INCR and GET.

sections.content:
### What to Focus On
* **Primary Objective**: Master the trade-offs between rate-limiting accuracy, computational overhead, memory footprint, and fault isolation when designing distributed throttling systems at scale (100,000+ QPS).
* **Key Decision Levers**:
  1. **Algorithmic Mechanics**: Sliding Window Counter vs Token Bucket vs Leaky Bucket vs Fixed Window.
  2. **Storage Architecture**: Centralized In-Memory Cluster (Redis) vs In-Process Memory Counters.
  3. **Resilience Policy Under Outages**: Fail-Open (prioritize availability) vs Fail-Closed (prioritize security & backend protection).
  4. **State Concurrency Control**: Atomic Lua Script vs Redis MULTI/EXEC vs Distributed Locking.
* **What You Should Be Able to Explain**:
  - Why fixed window algorithms permit up to $2\times$ burst traffic at boundary thresholds and how sliding window counters prevent it with $O(1)$ memory.
  - Why local in-memory counters multiply allowed traffic by the number of gateway instances ($N \times \text{limit}$).
  - How an atomic Redis Lua script executes counter incrementation and TTL expiration without race conditions.
  - How standard RFC headers (`X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `Retry-After`) guide client backoff behavior.
---

### Structured Decision Breakdown & Rationale

#### 1. Rate Limiting Algorithm: Sliding Window Counter vs Token Bucket vs Fixed Window
* **Option A: Fixed Window Counter**
  * **Optimizes For**: Lowest memory consumption ($1\text{ integer key}$ per window) and simplest implementation.
  * **Cost / Downside**: **Boundary Double-Burst Vulnerability**: A user can send $100\%$ of their quota at the last second of Window 1, and another $100\%$ at the first second of Window 2, resulting in $200\%$ allowable traffic within a 2-second interval, potentially crashing downstream databases.
  * **When to Choose**: Coarse-grained rate limiting (e.g., hourly quotas) where transient bursts do not impact backends.
* **Option B: Token Bucket**
  * **Optimizes For**: Smooth average rate enforcement while allowing controlled temporary traffic bursts up to bucket capacity.
  * **Cost / Downside**: Requires storing both token count and last-refill timestamp. If clients are idle, sudden bucket dumps can cause transient downstream queue spikes.
  * **When to Choose**: APIs where occasional bursty traffic (e.g. batch uploads, page loads) is natural and acceptable.
* **Option C: Sliding Window Counter (Approximation) [RECOMMENDED DEFAULT]**
  * **Optimizes For**: Mathematical prevention of boundary double-bursts with strictly $O(1)$ memory footprint. Calculates current rate using:
    $$\text{Rate} = \text{Count}_{\text{current}} + \text{Count}_{\text{previous}} \times (1 - \text{time elapsed in current window})$$
  * **Cost / Downside**: Assumes uniform distribution of requests across the previous window ($< 0.05\%$ error rate in practice).
  * **When to Choose**: High-throughput public APIs where accuracy is mandatory and memory efficiency across millions of concurrent users is critical.
* **Explicit Decision Rationale**: We select **Sliding Window Counter**. It completely eliminates the boundary burst problem of fixed windows while using only two counter keys per user, unlike Sliding Window Logs which store timestamps for every request and suffer $O(N)$ memory bloat.

#### 2. Storage Tier: Centralized Redis Cluster vs In-Process Memory
* **Option A: Centralized Redis Cluster [RECOMMENDED DEFAULT]**
  * **Optimizes For**: Globally coordinated accuracy. Every gateway instance evaluates against a single shared state.
  * **Cost / Downside**: Network round-trip ($0.5\text{--}1.5\text{ ms}$) added to the critical request path; dependency on Redis availability.
  * **When to Choose**: Multi-node gateway clusters where strict per-user or per-API-key quota enforcement is required.
* **Option B: Local In-Memory Counters (Process RAM)**
  * **Optimizes For**: Zero network latency ($< 1\mu\text{s}$) and zero external infrastructure dependencies.
  * **Cost / Downside**: **Traffic Multiplication Hazard**: Across a cluster of $M$ gateway nodes behind a round-robin load balancer, a client can consume up to $M \times \text{limit}$ requests because each node tracks quota independently without synchronization.
  * **When to Choose**: Single-instance microservices, or coarse Layer 4 DDoS filtering where approximate node-local limits suffice.
* **Explicit Decision Rationale**: We select **Centralized Redis Cluster**. In production systems with 20+ gateway instances, local memory would allow a malicious actor to exceed their quota by $20\times$. Redis provides sub-millisecond centralized accuracy.

#### 3. Outage Policy: Fail-Open vs Fail-Closed
* **Option A: Fail-Open (Allow Requests on Cache Down) [RECOMMENDED DEFAULT]**
  * **Optimizes For**: Maximizing availability and user experience during infrastructure incidents.
  * **Cost / Downside**: Exposes backend services to potential abuse or traffic spikes while rate limiting is degraded.
  * **When to Choose**: Public consumer applications, reading feeds, search queries, and general web traffic.
* **Option B: Fail-Closed (Block Requests on Cache Down)**
  * **Optimizes For**: Maximum security, financial safety, and fraud prevention.
  * **Cost / Downside**: An outage in Redis cascades into a total outage for all API traffic, blocking 100% of legitimate users.
  * **When to Choose**: Mission-critical billing endpoints, money transfers, password reset/login endpoints, and expensive third-party paid API proxy routes.
* **Explicit Decision Rationale**: We select **Fail-Open with Local Node Fallback** for general traffic, and **Fail-Closed** specifically for authentication and payment routes. A Redis hiccup should never prevent users from browsing, but should protect financial checkout pipelines.

#### 4. Concurrency & Atomicity: Lua Script vs MULTI/EXEC
* **Option A: Atomic Lua Script [RECOMMENDED DEFAULT]**
  * **Optimizes For**: Single-round-trip atomicity. Redis executes Lua scripts as a single atomic transaction without interleaving commands from other connections.
  * **Cost / Downside**: Long-running Lua scripts block the single-threaded Redis event loop (must be kept $< 1\text{ ms}$).
  * **When to Choose**: Rate limiting logic that requires reading the current count, incrementing, checking threshold, and setting expiration conditionally.
* **Option B: MULTI/EXEC (Optimistic Locking with WATCH)**
  * **Optimizes For**: Standard Redis commands without scripting.
  * **Cost / Downside**: If concurrent requests modify the key simultaneously, `EXEC` aborts and requires client-side retry loops, ballooning tail latency under high concurrency.
  * **When to Choose**: Low-concurrency workflows where write collisions are rare.
* **Explicit Decision Rationale**: We select **Atomic Lua Script**. Under viral traffic spikes where hundreds of concurrent requests arrive for the same user key, Lua guarantees atomic execution in a single network round-trip without retry loops or lock contention.

---

### Decision Comparison Tables

#### Table 1: Rate Limiting Algorithm Comparison
| Algorithm | Memory per Key | Time Complexity | Burst Handling | Boundary Surge Risk | Accuracy |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Fixed Window** | **$O(1)$ (1 integer)** | $O(1)$ | No (Strict limit) | **High ($2\times$ burst at edges)** | Low (Coarse) |
| **Token Bucket** | $O(1)$ (2 numbers) | $O(1)$ | **Yes (Up to capacity)** | Low | High |
| **Leaky Bucket** | $O(1)$ (Queue size) | $O(1)$ | No (Smooths traffic) | None (Constant outflow) | High |
| **Sliding Window Log** | $O(N)$ (All timestamps) | $O(N)$ | No | None | **100% Strict** |
| **Sliding Window Counter** | **$O(1)$ (2 integers)** | **$O(1)$** | Partial | **None ($< 0.05\%$ error)** | **Very High** |

#### Table 2: Storage Architecture Trade-Offs
| Characteristic | Centralized Redis Cluster | Local In-Memory (Node RAM) | Hybrid (Local Cache + Async Sync) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Rate Check Latency** | $0.8\text{--}2.0\text{ ms}$ | **$< 0.05\text{ ms}$** | $0.1\text{--}0.3\text{ ms}$ |
| **Multi-Node Quota Accuracy** | **100% Accurate** | Diverges by $N\times$ instances | Converges within sync interval |
| **Failure Blast Radius** | Redis outage impacts all limits | Node crash impacts only that node | Soft fallback to local estimates |
| **Network Egress Overhead** | 1 network hop per API request | Zero network calls | Periodic background sync packets |
| **Recommended Usage** | **Default Production Choice** | Single-node / Edge DDoS filters | Ultra-low latency enterprise APIs |

---

### Hidden Assumptions & Edge Realities
1. **Clock Synchronization (NTP)**: When using timestamps in Redis Lua scripts, ensure all Redis nodes and API gateway workers synchronize clocks via NTP; clock drift $> 1\text{ second}$ can distort sliding window weight calculations.
2. **Key Cardinality & Memory Sizing**: If tracking rate limits per IP address ($10\text{M}$ active IPs daily), each key using 100 bytes in Redis consumes $\sim 1\text{ GB}$ of RAM. Expire keys promptly with TTL ($`window + 60\text{s}`) to prevent memory leaks.
3. **Internal vs External Quotas**: Unauthenticated public endpoints should be throttled by client IP; authenticated API endpoints must be throttled by `AccountID` or `APIKey`, as multiple enterprise users often share corporate NAT IP addresses.

---

### Common Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
* **The Boundary Double-Burst Outage**: Implementing fixed-window rate limiting on a $1,000\text{ req/sec}$ tier, only to suffer a $2,000\text{ req/sec}$ surge when a bot fires requests across the second boundary ($:59.999$ and $:00.001$).
* **Thundering Herd When Rate Limiter Fails**: Failing closed when Redis encounters a network hiccup, causing the gateway to reject $100\%$ of legitimate user traffic and transforming a minor cache slowdown into a company-wide outage.
* **Missing Standard Retry-After Headers**: Returning a raw `HTTP 429` without `Retry-After` or `X-RateLimit-Reset` headers, causing aggressive client SDKs to enter a tight infinite retry loop that intensifies the Denial of Service.
* **Client IP Spoofing via Header Forgery**: Extracting client IP directly from `X-Forwarded-For` without validating that the header was stripped and reset by your perimeter load balancer, allowing attackers to bypass rate limits by injecting random spoofed IPs.

---

### Concrete Implementation Examples & Payloads

#### 1. Atomic Sliding Window Lua Script (Redis Execution)
```lua
-- KEYS[1]: Current window key (e.g. rate:user123:1730419200)
-- KEYS[2]: Previous window key (e.g. rate:user123:1730419140)
-- ARGV[1]: Max limit (e.g. 100)
-- ARGV[2]: Current timestamp in seconds
-- ARGV[3]: Window size in seconds (e.g. 60)

local current_key = KEYS[1]
local prev_key = KEYS[2]
local limit = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local now = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local window = tonumber(ARGV[3])

local current_count = tonumber(redis.call('GET', current_key) or "0")
local prev_count = tonumber(redis.call('GET', prev_key) or "0")

local time_into_current_window = now % window
local weight = (window - time_into_current_window) / window
local estimated_count = current_count + (prev_count * weight)

if estimated_count >= limit then
  return {0, math.ceil(limit - estimated_count), window - time_into_current_window}
else
  redis.call('INCR', current_key)
  if current_count == 0 then
    redis.call('EXPIRE', current_key, window * 2)
  end
  return {1, math.floor(limit - estimated_count - 1), 0}
end
```

#### 2. Allowed Request Headers (Within Quota)
```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
X-RateLimit-Limit: 100
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 74
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1730419260

{
  "status": "success",
  "data": { ... }
}
```

#### 3. Quota Exceeded Response (HTTP 429 Short-Circuit)
```http
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Content-Type: application/json
Retry-After: 26
X-RateLimit-Limit: 100
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1730419260

{
  "error": "too_many_requests",
  "message": "API rate limit exceeded for plan 'Standard'. Please retry in 26 seconds.",
  "retryAfterSeconds": 26
}
```

stages.learnerPrompt: What happens during a Redis node failure? How do you handle hot users who generate millions of requests? How do you enforce limits for a user distributed across 5 geographic regions?

failureModes: Redis node failure: With Redis Sentinel or Cluster, replica promotion takes 10–30 s. During that window: fail-open (allow) or local fallback counter (allow up to local_limit = limit/node_count). Redis Cluster with consistent hashing for key distribution — each userId is pinned to one shard.

Hot user: A single userId key in Redis becomes a hot key, concentrating load on one Redis shard. Mitigation: replicate hot keys to N replicas and read-balance across them; or shard the counter across K sub-keys (userId:0..K-1) and sum them — introduces K reads per request.

Cross-region rate limiting: Each region maintains its own Redis counter. Eventual synchronization via async replication — allows up to sum(regional_limits) globally. True global rate limiting requires a global counter service (high latency) or token-bucket with quota allocation per region.

stages.learnerPrompt: New requirement: the API has 3 tiers — free (100 req/min), pro (1,000 req/min), enterprise (unlimited). Enterprise customers also get burst headroom of 50% for up to 10 seconds. How do you model this? Where does tier information come from?

approachSteps: 1. Resolve tier from API key on each request — cache the key→tier mapping in local memory (5-minute TTL) to avoid DB round-trips.
2. Look up limit for the resolved tier from a config store (environment variable, feature flag service, or DB with in-process cache).
3. For enterprise burst: maintain a separate burst counter with a 10-second TTL. Allow up to limit * 1.5 for the burst window, then enforce normal limit.
4. Pass the effective limit into the sliding window counter logic — same algorithm, different threshold.
tradeOffs: Local API-key→tier cache: reduces DB load but has up to 5-minute lag on tier changes (acceptable for most plan upgrades).

Enterprise unlimited: skip the rate limiter entirely for unlimited-tier keys — reduces Redis calls. Risk: runaway client bugs consume infrastructure. Recommended: enforce a very high soft limit (e.g., 1M/min) and alert rather than truly unlimited.

spark.summary: A distributed rate limiter controls how many requests a user, API key, or IP address can make within a time window. It protects backend services from overload and abuse while keeping legitimate traffic available. The distributed challenge is sharing quota state across many API servers without adding too much latency.
spark.keyTakeaway: Put the limiter at the API gateway, keep policy configuration close to the request path, and use an atomic shared counter store such as Redis. Choose the algorithm, consistency scope, and outage behavior explicitly.

problem.title: Design a Distributed Rate Limiter
problem.prompt: Design a rate limiter for a public API that enforces per-user and per-IP request limits at scale. The service must handle high throughput, be deployable across multiple data center regions, and gracefully degrade when the rate-limiting backend is unavailable.
requirements: Enforce per-user and per-IP rate limits, such as 1,000 requests per minute per user.
Return HTTP 429 with retry guidance when a quota is exceeded.
Support per-second, per-minute, and per-hour windows.
Coordinate decisions across multiple API server instances.
Support configurable limits by API key tier and endpoint.
Define fail-open or fail-closed behavior when the rate-limit store is unavailable.
constraints: Peak API traffic is approximately 500,000 requests per second.
Rate-limit decisions should add no more than 2 ms at p99.
The limiter should provide shared enforcement across 10 or more API nodes in a region.
API processes do not share memory.
Regional enforcement is the default scope; strict global enforcement requires additional coordination.

concept.whyItMatters: Without a rate limiter, a small number of clients can consume disproportionate backend capacity, trigger cascading failures, or abuse expensive API operations. A single-server counter is insufficient when requests are distributed across many API nodes because each node would maintain an independent quota. The limiter therefore needs shared state, low-latency decisions, and an explicit policy for backend failures.
whenToUse: Public APIs exposed to unknown or untrusted clients.
Expensive endpoints such as search, reporting, export, or authentication APIs.
Multi-tenant systems that need fair-use quotas by user, API key, organization, or IP address.
Services that must protect downstream dependencies from sudden traffic spikes.
whenNotToUse: As the only defense against volumetric DDoS attacks.
When a local, deterministic limit is sufficient and requests never cross process boundaries.
When blocking or delaying requests would be more harmful than allowing temporary excess traffic.
When the limit must be a strict global transaction across regions but no global coordination mechanism is available.
keyPoints: The API gateway is a natural enforcement point because it can reject requests before they reach backend services.
A distributed counter is required when multiple API nodes share one logical quota.
The check and counter update must be atomic to prevent concurrent requests from exceeding the limit.
Redis is suitable for short-lived counter state because it provides low-latency operations, TTLs, clustering, and server-side Lua scripts.
A sliding-window counter is a practical default because it uses constant-size state and reduces fixed-window boundary bursts.
Token bucket is preferable when the product needs explicit burst capacity and a sustained refill rate.
Fail-open protects availability but permits excess traffic during an outage.
Fail-closed protects the backend and sensitive operations but can block legitimate clients during an outage.
Regional enforcement is simpler and faster than strict global enforcement.
A local counter on every API node can allow approximately N times the intended quota when N nodes independently admit traffic.

terms.definition: A policy that restricts how many operations an identity may perform during a period.
The maximum number of requests allowed by a policy.
A request whose policy or counter state is available from the expected low-latency store.
A counter that resets at fixed boundaries such as 12:00:00, 12:01:00, and 12:02:00.
An approximate rolling count calculated from the current window and a weighted previous-window count.
A limiter that replenishes tokens at a configured rate up to a maximum capacity.
Allow the request when the rate-limit backend is unavailable.
Reject or block the request when the rate-limit backend is unavailable.

tradeOffs.pro: A sliding-window counter reduces boundary bursts while keeping constant-size state.
tradeOffs.con: It estimates the rolling count and does not provide an exact error percentage for every traffic pattern.

tradeOffs.pro: A sliding-window counter is straightforward for fixed quotas; a token bucket expresses burst capacity naturally.
tradeOffs.con: The sliding-window counter does not model burst capacity as explicitly as a token bucket.

tradeOffs.pro: Redis provides shared state across API nodes.
tradeOffs.con: Redis introduces a network dependency and additional latency. Local memory is faster but independently counts traffic on each node.

tradeOffs.pro: Fail-open preserves availability when Redis is unavailable.
tradeOffs.con: Fail-open allows unchecked traffic and may expose backend services to abuse. Fail-closed protects the backend but may reject legitimate clients.

tradeOffs.pro: Regional enforcement keeps latency low and avoids cross-region coordination.
tradeOffs.con: Independent regional quotas can exceed a single global allowance. Strict global enforcement requires coordination and reduces availability during partitions.

tradeOffs.pro: A Lua script keeps read, decision, increment, and expiration logic together on the Redis server.
tradeOffs.con: Lua scripts must remain short and carefully validated because they execute synchronously in Redis.

failureModes.name: Independent local counters
failureModes.description: Each API node maintains its own counter, so a client can receive a separate quota from every node.
failureModes.mitigation: Use shared regional state or explicitly bound local quota allocation.

failureModes.name: Fixed-window boundary burst
failureModes.description: A client sends its full quota at the end of one window and another full quota at the beginning of the next.
failureModes.mitigation: Use a sliding-window counter, token bucket, or sliding-window log.

failureModes.name: Redis unavailable
failureModes.description: The gateway cannot determine whether the request is within quota.
failureModes.mitigation: Choose fail-open or fail-closed by endpoint. Add timeouts, circuit breakers, local protection, and load shedding where appropriate.

failureModes.name: Hot identity
failureModes.description: A single user or API key maps to one Redis shard and produces disproportionate traffic.
failureModes.mitigation: Use coarse local protection or bounded quota leases. More shards do not automatically split one hot key.

failureModes.name: Global quota drift
failureModes.description: Independent regional counters each admit the full quota, multiplying the effective global allowance.
failureModes.mitigation: Allocate regional budgets whose sum stays within the global allowance, or use a coordinated global limiter.

failureModes.name: Race between read and increment
failureModes.description: Concurrent requests read the same counter before either request updates it.
failureModes.mitigation: Use a Redis Lua script to perform the read, decision, increment, and expiration atomically.

failureModes.name: Untrusted client IP
failureModes.description: A client spoofs forwarding headers or many users share one NAT address.
failureModes.mitigation: Trust forwarded headers only from controlled proxies and combine IP limits with authenticated identity limits.

commonMistakes: Using an independent in-memory counter on every API node and calling it a distributed limiter.
Assuming a sliding-window counter is exact for every request distribution.
Claiming that more Redis shards automatically solve a hot identity.
Reading counters from replicas for an authoritative admission decision.
Using a database counter on every request despite a strict latency budget.
Failing open globally without assessing backend abuse risk.
Failing closed globally without considering legitimate traffic and availability.
Treating regional limits as strict global limits.
Performing Redis reads and writes separately without atomicity.
Ignoring tenant, user, endpoint, or API-key identity when constructing counter keys.
Returning HTTP 429 for a backend outage when the client did not actually exceed its quota.
Measuring only average latency instead of p99 latency, timeouts, denials, fallback activation, memory, and shard skew.

sections.content:
## Protect the backend before forwarding the request

A rate limiter decides whether a request should continue to the backend. It normally runs at the API gateway, where it can reject excess traffic before that traffic consumes application, database, or downstream-service capacity.

The distributed requirement changes the design. If ten API nodes each keep a local counter, a client may receive ten independent quotas. Shared state is required when the quota is defined across the whole region rather than per process.

The main design tension is **accuracy versus latency versus availability**.

sections.label: Interview answer
sections.content: We need shared per-user and per-IP limits, configurable by plan and endpoint. Before designing, I’ll clarify whether bursts are allowed, whether limits must be globally exact, and which routes should fail open during an outage.

## Requirements and constraints

### Functional requirements

- Enforce per-user and per-IP limits.
- Support per-second, per-minute, and per-hour windows.
- Configure quotas by plan, endpoint, and identity.
- Return HTTP 429 when a quota is exceeded.
- Return retry guidance to clients.
- Define outage behavior per endpoint.

### Capacity constraints

- Peak traffic is approximately 500,000 requests per second.
- Rate-limit decisions should add no more than 2 ms at p99.
- The limiter must coordinate decisions across 10 or more regional API nodes.
- API processes do not share memory.
- Regional enforcement is the default scope.

## Estimate the critical path

Assume 10 million active identity-policy pairs and approximately 200 bytes of primary state per pair for two window counters. That gives roughly 2 GB of primary counter state before replicas, allocator overhead, and capacity headroom.

Checking both user and IP limits across three windows can produce up to six policy evaluations per request.

At an illustrative measured capacity of 50,000 policy evaluations per second per Redis shard, one evaluation per request would require approximately ten primary shards before headroom.

These are sizing assumptions. Benchmark the actual Lua script, network latency, queueing, hot-key skew, failover behavior, and p99 latency before finalizing capacity.

sections.expression:
policy evaluations/sec = requests/sec × policies checked
primary shards ≈ ceil(policy evaluations/sec ÷ measured capacity per shard)

sections.content:
## Request flow

1. The client sends an API request.
2. The API gateway extracts the authenticated user, API key, and trusted client IP.
3. The gateway loads the applicable policy from its local configuration cache.
4. The gateway checks and updates the distributed counters.
5. If all required policies allow the request, the gateway forwards it to the backend.
6. If any policy rejects the request, the gateway returns HTTP 429.

## Storage model

Redis stores short-lived counter state. A durable configuration store stores rate-limit policies, which are cached at the gateway.

A counter key may look like:

`rl:{user:42}:read:60:{windowStart}`

The identity is included in the key, along with the endpoint, window length, and window start. Keys accessed by one Lua script must share a Redis Cluster hash slot.

Counter keys should expire after approximately twice their window length so inactive identities do not remain indefinitely.

sections.content:
## Sliding-window counter

The limiter stores a counter for the current window and a counter for the previous window. It weights the previous counter according to the portion of that window that still overlaps the current time.

The estimate is:

`estimate = current + previous × (1 − elapsed / window)`

The next request is allowed only when:

`estimate + 1 ≤ limit`

This approach uses constant-size state and reduces the boundary burst problem of fixed windows. It is still an approximation: it assumes requests from the previous window were distributed reasonably across that window.

sections.title: Atomic sliding-window counter
sections.content:
-- KEYS[1]: current window key
-- KEYS[2]: previous window key
-- Both keys must share a Redis Cluster hash slot.
-- ARGV: limit, now in seconds, window in seconds

local limit = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local now = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local window = tonumber(ARGV[3])

local current = tonumber(redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) or "0")
local previous = tonumber(redis.call("GET", KEYS[2]) or "0")

local elapsed = now % window
local estimate = current + previous * (1 - elapsed / window)

if estimate + 1 > limit then
  local retry = math.max(1, math.ceil(2 * window - elapsed))
  return {0, 0, retry}
end

redis.call("INCR", KEYS[1])
redis.call("EXPIRE", KEYS[1], 2 * window)

local remaining = math.max(0, math.floor(limit - estimate - 1))
return {1, remaining, 0}

## API contract

The internal limiter can expose:

`check(identity, policyId) → { allowed, remaining, retryAfterSeconds }`

For a quota violation, return HTTP 429:

- `Retry-After: 26`
- `X-RateLimit-Limit: 1000`
- `X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0`

The response body may be:

```json
{
  "error": "rate_limit_exceeded",
  "retryAfterSeconds": 26
}
```

If Redis is unavailable and the endpoint uses a fail-closed policy, return HTTP 503 rather than incorrectly claiming that the client exceeded its quota.

sections.title: Atomic Redis token bucket alternative
sections.content:
-- Atomic Redis Token Bucket Script
local tokens_key = KEYS[1]
local timestamp_key = KEYS[2]

local rate = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local requested = tonumber(ARGV[4])

local current_tokens = tonumber(redis.call('get', tokens_key))
local last_refreshed = tonumber(redis.call('get', timestamp_key))

if current_tokens == nil then
  current_tokens = capacity
  last_refreshed = now
end

local delta = math.max(0, now - last_refreshed)
local tokens = math.min(capacity, current_tokens + (delta * rate))

if tokens >= requested then
  redis.call('set', tokens_key, tokens - requested)
  redis.call('set', timestamp_key, now)
  redis.call('expire', tokens_key, 3600)
  redis.call('expire', timestamp_key, 3600)
  return 1
else
  return 0
end

## Why atomicity matters

A non-atomic implementation might read the current count, decide that the request is allowed, and increment later. Concurrent requests can all observe the same old count and collectively exceed the quota.

A Redis Lua script performs the read, decision, increment, and expiration as one server-side operation. Redis executes the script atomically relative to other commands.

`MULTI/EXEC` executes queued commands atomically, but client-side decisions made between separate reads and writes can still race. `WATCH` provides optimistic concurrency and may require retries.

## Failure handling

### Fail open

Allow requests when Redis is unavailable.

Use this for availability-sensitive routes where temporary excess traffic is preferable to blocking legitimate users. Add local protection, circuit breakers, and high-priority monitoring when appropriate.

The risk is that abuse can continue without shared enforcement during the outage.

### Fail closed

Reject or block requests when Redis is unavailable.

Use this for sensitive routes such as authentication, billing, or expensive operations where unchecked traffic could cause serious harm.

The risk is that legitimate traffic is rejected during a rate-limit backend failure.

The policy should be selected per endpoint rather than applied globally.

## Multiple regions

Independent regional limiters improve latency and availability but do not automatically enforce one strict global quota. If every region receives the full quota, the effective global allowance becomes approximately:

`global allowance ≈ regional quota × number of active regions`

A bounded alternative is to allocate regional budgets whose sum remains within the global quota. This can waste capacity when traffic is unevenly distributed.

Strict global coordination provides stronger enforcement but adds cross-region latency and creates harder availability decisions during partitions.

## What to monitor and test

Monitor:

- Rate-check p99 latency.
- Allowed and denied requests.
- Redis timeouts and errors.
- Circuit-breaker state.
- Fail-open and fail-closed activations.
- Redis memory usage.
- Shard skew and hot keys.
- Policy-cache age and refresh failures.

Test:

- Concurrent requests for one identity.
- Requests around window boundaries.
- Policy changes and cache invalidation.
- Redis failover.
- Clock skew.
- Regional traffic imbalance.
- One hot user or API key.
- Simultaneous per-user and per-IP rejection.

## The 30-second answer

Put the limiter at the API gateway, cache rate-limit policies locally, and use regional Redis with an atomic Lua operation for shared counter state. Start with a sliding-window counter because it provides constant-size state and reduces fixed-window boundary bursts. Return HTTP 429 with Retry-After when a request exceeds its quota. Choose fail-open or fail-closed behavior per endpoint. Treat strict global quotas as a separate design decision because they require coordination across regions.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Design a Distributed Rate Limiter

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: A distributed rate limiter controls how many requests a user, API key, or IP address can make within a time window. It protects backend services from overload and abuse while keeping legitimate traffic available. The distributed challenge is sharing quota state across many API servers without adding too much latency.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Rate Limiter applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Local Policy Cache.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Redis node failure: With Redis Sentinel or Cluster, replica promotion takes 10–30 s. During that window: fail-open (allow) or local fallback counter (allow up to local_limit = limit/node_count). Redis Cluster with consistent hashing for key distribution — each userId is pinned to one shard.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Sliding window vs fixed window: Fixed window allows up to 2× burst at the boundary (last second of window N + first second of window N+1). Sliding window eliminates this at O(1) memory cost.

tipsAndTricks: Interview anchor: Put the limiter at the API gateway, keep policy configuration close to the request path, and use an atomic shared counter store such as Redis. Choose the algorithm, consistency scope, and outage behavior explicitly.

Trade-off tip: Sliding window vs fixed window: Fixed window allows up to 2× burst at the boundary (last second of window N + first second of window N+1). Sliding window eliminates this at O(1) memory cost.
Trade-off tip: Redis vs local counter: Local is O(0ms) but each node allows limit requests independently — 10 nodes allow 10× limit. Redis adds ~1 ms but provides a shared accurate counter.

Watch out for: Redis node failure: With Redis Sentinel or Cluster, replica promotion takes 10–30 s. During that window: fail-open (allow) or local fallback counter (allow up to local_limit = limit/node_count). Redis Cluster with consistent hashing for key distribution — each userId is pinned to one shard.

Watch out for: Hot user: A single userId key in Redis becomes a hot key, concentrating load on one Redis shard. Mitigation: replicate hot keys to N replicas and read-balance across them; or shard the counter across K sub-keys (userId:0..K-1) and sum them — introduces K reads per request.
